k-magnitude-s1.title: Equilibrium constants for four reactions
k-magnitude-s1.text: A student looks up Kc for four gas-phase reactions, each at 25 °C. Each reaction starts with only its reactants, at 1.0 M each.

k-magnitude-s2.title: Three reactions at equilibrium
k-magnitude-s2.html:
Key: X2Y2XY

Each container shows a different reaction of the form X2(g) + Y2(g) ⇌ 2 XY(g) at equilibrium. The containers have equal volumes and each started with 5 X2 and 5 Y2.

items.q: In which reaction does the equilibrium mixture contain almost nothing but reactants?
options: Reaction 1
Reaction 2
Reaction 3
Reaction 4

why.correct: The smaller K is, the less product the equilibrium mixture contains. K = 10⁻³¹ means the reaction barely proceeds.
options: Right: K = 4.5 × 10⁻³¹ is extremely small, so at equilibrium the product, NO, is present in a tiny amount.
K = 2.5 × 10³³ is huge: this reaction goes essentially to products.
K = 1.0 × 10⁵ is large, so products are favored.
K = 4.6 × 10⁻³ is small, so reactants are favored, but not nearly as strongly as in reaction 1.

items.q: The student concludes that reaction 2 must reach equilibrium within seconds because its K is so large. Is the conclusion justified?
options: No: K shows where equilibrium lies, not how fast it is reached.
Yes: a large K means a large rate constant for the forward reaction.
Yes: products form quickly whenever K is greater than 1.
No: a large K means the reaction is slow, because the reverse reaction is fast.

why.correct: K describes the mixture once equilibrium is reached. How long that takes is kinetics (Unit 5). H₂ and Cl₂ can sit mixed in the dark for a long time, then react explosively in sunlight; K is the same either way.
options: Right: K is about the composition at equilibrium. Speed depends on the activation energy and the rate law, which K does not tell you.
K compares forward and reverse at equilibrium; a large K is compatible with both reactions being very slow.
Being product-favored says how much product there will be, not when. Some product-favored reactions take years.
K does not set the speed in either direction, so it cannot tell you the reaction is slow either.

items.q: Which reaction in the table is the most product-favored at equilibrium?
options: Reaction 2
Reaction 3
Reaction 4
Reaction 1

why.correct: Compare exponents: the reaction with the largest K has the most product relative to reactant at equilibrium.
options: Right: it has the largest K, 2.5 × 10³³.
K = 1.0 × 10⁵ is large, but 10³³ is far larger.
K = 4.6 × 10⁻³ is below 1, so reaction 4 favors reactants.
Reaction 1 has the smallest K in the table; it favors reactants overwhelmingly.

items.q: For reaction 4, a student starts with 1.0 M N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> and predicts that almost all of it will turn into NO<sub>2</sub>. Which response is best?
options: The prediction is wrong: K < 1, so most N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> remains at equilibrium.
The prediction is right: N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> is the one species present at the start.
The prediction is right: K is positive, so products are favored.
The prediction is wrong: no NO<sub>2</sub> forms, because K is less than 1.

why.correct: K much less than 1 means reactants are favored: some product forms, but most of the reactant is still there at equilibrium.
options: Right: K = 4.6 × 10⁻³. With [N₂O₄] near 1.0 M, [NO₂]² ≈ 4.6 × 10⁻³, so [NO₂] ≈ 0.068 M: a few percent reacts.
Starting with reactant only tells you the net reaction is forward (Q = 0 < K). It does not tell you how far it goes.
Every K is positive. What matters is whether K is much larger or much smaller than 1.
K < 1 does not mean zero product. Some NO₂ forms, just not much.

items.q: Which reaction has the largest equilibrium constant?
options: Reaction I
Reaction II
Reaction III
They are equal, because each started with the same amounts.

why.correct: The equilibrium mixture with the most product relative to reactant has the largest K. Count: I has 8 XY to 1 + 1 reactant molecules.
options: Right: K = 8² / (1 × 1) = 64, by far the most product per reactant.
K = 2² / (4 × 4) = 0.25, the smallest of the three.
K = 4² / (3 × 3) ≈ 1.8, in between.
Same starting amounts but different reactions settle at different mixtures, so the K values differ.

items.q: Each particle in a container stands for 0.10 mol, and each container is 1.0 L. Calculate K<sub>c</sub> for reaction II.

mistakes.why: Value: [XY] is squared, because its coefficient is 2.
Value: you inverted K. Products go on top.

items.q: Which statement about reaction II is correct?
options: Its K is less than 1, so reactants are favored.
Its K is greater than 1, because product is present.
It is not at equilibrium, because it has more reactant than product.
It will react further toward products, because K is small.

why.correct: A small K describes an equilibrium mixture that is mostly reactants. It is still an equilibrium: no further net change.
options: Right: K = 0.25, and the box holds 8 reactant molecules for every 2 product molecules.
Any equilibrium mixture contains some product. K > 1 needs products to outweigh reactants in the ratio, which they do not here.
The question says each container is at equilibrium. Mostly-reactant mixtures are common equilibria.
At equilibrium, Q = K and there is no net reaction, whatever the size of K.

items.q: Reaction III is at equilibrium. Which statement compares its forward and reverse rates?
options: They are equal, even though K is not 1.
The forward rate is larger, because K is greater than 1.
The reverse rate is larger, because there are more reactant molecules.
Both rates are zero, because the composition has stopped changing.

why.correct: At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal, whatever the value of K. K describes the composition; the equal rates describe the dynamics.
options: Right: equal rates define equilibrium for every reaction; K > 1 or K < 1 only describes where the amounts end up.
K > 1 means more product at equilibrium, not a larger forward rate at equilibrium. At equilibrium the rates are equal.
If the reverse rate were larger, the composition would still be changing. It is at equilibrium.
Constant composition comes from equal rates, not zero rates.

items.q: For a reaction at 25 °C, K = 6.0 × 10<sup>−9</sup>. Which describes the equilibrium mixture?
options: Mostly reactants, with a very small amount of products
Mostly products, with a very small amount of reactants
Equal amounts of reactants and products
No products whatsoever

why.correct: K ≪ 1: reactant-favored. Some product is present at equilibrium, but very little.
options: Right: K far below 1 means the reaction barely goes forward before it reaches equilibrium.
That would need K far above 1.
K near 1 gives comparable amounts; 10⁻⁹ is very far from 1.
A small K still means some product forms. K is never zero.

items.q: For a reaction, K = 3 × 10<sup>12</sup>. Which statements are justified? Select all that apply.
options: At equilibrium, products are favored.
Starting from reactants, the reaction goes nearly to completion.
The reaction is fast.
At equilibrium, the forward rate is larger than the reverse rate.

why.correct: A large K means products dominate the equilibrium mixture. It does not tell you how fast equilibrium is reached, and at equilibrium the rates are always equal.
options: Right: K far greater than 1.
Right: with K this large, very little reactant is left at equilibrium.
K says nothing about rate. A product-favored reaction can be very slow.
At equilibrium the two rates are equal, whatever K is.

items.q: For A(g) ⇌ 2 B(g), K<sub>c</sub> = 1.0 × 10<sup>−5</sup>. Because K is so small, almost all of the A remains when equilibrium is reached from 0.10 M A. Using [A] ≈ 0.10 M at equilibrium, estimate [B].

mistakes.why: Value: that is [B]². Take the square root to get [B].
Value: set K = [B]² / [A] and solve for [B]; do not divide by the coefficient.

why.correct: K = [B]² / [A], so [B]² ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.10 = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ and [B] ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻³ M. That is about 0.5% of the A reacting, which confirms [A] ≈ 0.10 M was a fair approximation.

items.q: A cylinder of H<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub> gases can stand for years without forming water, though K for 2 H<sub>2</sub>(g) + O<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 H<sub>2</sub>O(g) is enormous at room temperature. What explains this?
options: The reaction has a high activation energy, so it is extremely slow at room temperature.
The mixture is already at equilibrium.
K is large, so the reverse reaction prevents water from forming.
K applies once some water has already formed.

why.correct: Thermodynamics (the size of K) and kinetics (the rate) are separate. A large K tells you where the reaction would end, not that it will get there quickly.
options: Right: K says water is overwhelmingly favored at equilibrium, but without a spark or catalyst very few collisions get over the energy barrier.
At equilibrium with K this large, there would be almost no H₂ and O₂ left. The cylinder is far from equilibrium.
A large K favors the forward reaction. The reverse reaction is negligible.
K applies to the reaction at any composition; Q = 0 here, so the net reaction should go forward. It just goes very slowly.

items.q: Which value of K describes a reaction in which significant amounts of both reactants and products are present at equilibrium?

why.correct: When K is near 1 (roughly between 10⁻³ and 10³ is a common guide), the equilibrium mixture holds appreciable amounts of both reactants and products.
options: Right: K close to 1 means neither side dominates.
This K is huge: products dominate.
This K is tiny: reactants dominate.
Products dominate when K is billions.

items.q: For reaction P, K = 1 × 10<sup>4</sup>; for reaction R, K = 1 × 10<sup>−4</sup>. Both start with only reactants. Which statement is correct?
options: P ends with mostly products and R with mostly reactants.
P reaches equilibrium faster than R.
P ends with mostly reactants and R with mostly products.
Both end with equal amounts of reactants and products.

why.correct: K above 1 means product-favored; K below 1 means reactant-favored. Speed is a separate question.
options: Right: K far above 1 favors products; K far below 1 favors reactants.
K does not tell you which reaction is faster.
This reverses the meaning of K: a larger K means more product.
Only a K near 1 gives comparable amounts; these are 10⁴ and 10⁻⁴.

items.q: A student writes: "K for this reaction is 10<sup>−6</sup>, so no reaction occurs and there is nothing to study." Which response is best?
options: Disagree: a little product forms before equilibrium.
Agree: a K below 10<sup>−3</sup> means the reaction does not happen.
Disagree: a small K means the reaction is fast, so it reaches equilibrium at once.
Agree: K is so small that the reverse reaction stops the forward one.

why.correct: Every reversible reaction forms some product. A small K means the equilibrium mixture contains only a little of it.
options: Right: K ≪ 1 means little product, not none. Small K reactions still reach a dynamic equilibrium.
There is no cutoff below which nothing reacts. The forward reaction runs until its rate equals the reverse rate.
K says nothing about speed.
The reverse reaction does not stop the forward reaction; at equilibrium both run at equal rates.

items.q: For the same reaction, which statement about K and Q is correct?
options: K is fixed at a given temperature; Q changes as the mixture changes.
Q is fixed at a given temperature; K changes as the mixture changes.
Both change as the mixture changes.
Neither changes once the reactants are mixed.

why.correct: K depends only on temperature for a given reaction. Q depends on the amounts present at the moment.
options: Right: Q tracks the current mixture and moves toward K.
This is reversed. K is the constant; Q varies.
K does not change with the mixture, only with temperature.
Q changes as the reaction runs, until it equals K.
